bib.title: The Winograd Schema Challenge
bib.venue: Proceedings of the Thirteenth International Conference on Principles of Knowledge Representation and Reasoning (KR 2012), pp. 552-561; copyright AAAI 2012

question: Can a test of pronoun-disambiguation questions that need world knowledge replace the Turing Test as a clear-cut, automatically gradable measure of intelligent behaviour?
hypothesis: Answering Winograd schemas at near-human accuracy requires background knowledge and reasoning that cannot be got from selectional restrictions or corpus statistics alone.
contributions: Define the Winograd schema: a sentence pair differing in one or two words with a pronoun ambiguity resolved in opposite directions
Propose the Winograd Schema Challenge as an alternative to the Turing Test
Give a collection of more than 100 schemas, 37 shown in the appendix

results.claim: A 50-question test should be enough to rule out guessing and takes a person about 25 minutes.
results.setup: Proposed test administration; no experiment run
results.quote: A test with 50 questions should only take a person 25 minutes or so to complete.

results.claim: A word list of about 500 words (give or take proper names) should suffice to publish ahead of a 50-question test.
results.setup: Proposed vocabulary release for a 50-question test
results.quote: For a test with 50 questions, which should be enough to rule out mere guessing, 500 words (give or take proper names) should be sufficient.

results.claim: Passing requires near-human accuracy, presumably close to 100% if schemas are easy for humans.
results.setup: Hidden corpus of Winograd schemas, one sentence from each pair; no system evaluated
results.quote: presumably close to 100%, if constraint (1) above has been satisfied by the corpus designers

results.claim: Building a hand-crafted set of about 100 schemas costs one or two weeks of work.
results.quote: the labor involved in constructing a small dataset of around 100 examples is on the order of one or two weeks of work

results.claim: The library available online holds more than 100 schemas.
results.quote: a collection of more than 100 examples can be found at

results.claim: The Loebner competition gives judges only 5 minutes per conversation, cited as too little to see past canned small talk.
results.quote: the Loebner competition gives judges only 5 minutes to determine whether or not they are conversing with a person or a computer (Christian 2011)

results.claim: Worked example: swapping one word (big/small) flips the referent of 'it' in the trophy sentence, so word-order and word-association tricks fail.
results.setup: Trophy/suitcase schema, special word big, alternate small
results.quote: Contexts where "give" can appear are statistically quite similar to those where "receive" can appear, and yet the answer must change.

limits: No system is run and no accuracy, human or machine, is reported; the claims are design arguments.
Authors concede the schemas are artificial and expensive to build, so large or frequently refreshed sets are impractical (Sec 10.3).
Appendix Google-count experiments are not reported and the authors say to take them with several grains of salt.

Authors say they will not provide training annotations and the challenge is agnostic to knowledge-based vs statistical approaches; the paper expects knowledge-based methods to be the likelier route, which later supervised and LLM results on WSC-style data dated.
Authors concede answers not being on the web is assumed for the Google-proof claim; the schemas were later published (Appendix links a public page).
A hand-picked 'obvious to humans' criterion is untested empirically: the paper says candidate questions must be tested before use but reports no human study.
Authors state the strongest claim (passing means thinking) would need a philosophical defence, and make only the weaker behavioural claim.

terms.definition: A pair of sentences differing in only one or two words and containing an ambiguity that is resolved in opposite ways in the two sentences and that requires the use of world knowledge and reasoning for its resolution.
A word appearing in the sentence that, when replaced by another word (the alternate), leaves everything making sense but changes the answer.
There should be no obvious statistical test over text corpora that will reliably disambiguate these correctly.
Constraints on which entities can fill a predicate (only women can be pregnant, only pills carcinogenic); schemas must not be solvable by them.

lineage.note: Challenge proposed as an alternative that keeps the behavioural stance without deception
Town councillors/demonstrators example is the origin of the schema
Argued RTE rests on a fuzzy entailment notion and tests shallow inference
Causal-choice benchmark; less clear-cut and narrower than WS
